newsitem.title: UK: UK's Telegraph sees circulation dispute resolution.
newsitem.headline: UK's Telegraph sees circulation dispute resolution.

text.p: The Telegraph Group, publisher of Britain's Daily Telegraph and Sunday Telegraph newspapers, said it was optimistic of soon resolving a dispute with the Audit Bureau of Circulation over its subscription figures.
"Representatives of the Audit Bureau of Circulation Ltd have had a full-day meeting with the Telegraph Group," Patrick Barrow, a spokesman for the Telegraph, told Reuters on Wednesday.

"Following constructive discussions, both sides are optimistic that the current position concerning circulation figures for the Telegraph Group titles will be resolved prior to the publication of the December ABC figures."

The Telegraph, owned by Canada's Hollinger International Inc, has been locked in a dispute with the audit bureau since the bureau said it would count the Telegraph's discounted subscriptions as sales at a lower rate.
The Telegraph raised a legal challenge, and the audit bureau ultimately published its November circulation figures last week without any figures for the Telegraph newspapers.

Underscoring the dispute is the Telegraph's hotly contested efforts to maintain the Daily Telegraph's standing as the largest-circulating broadsheet newspaper in Britain at the same time that its arch-rival the Times -- part of Rupert Murdoch's News Corp Ltd empire -- saw its circulation soar on a recent promotion which offered free tickets on the cross-Channel Eurostar train.
The Times has also led the way with cover price cuts, selling the newspaper for 10 pence on Mondays, versus 35 pence on other weekdays and 50 pence on Saturday.
The audit bureau last week reported that the Times had November circulatio of 861,931.
The Telegraph said audit figures by accounting and consultancy group KPMG put total circulation for the Daily Telegraph at 1.1 million in November.

The Telegraph, meanwhile, whose first-ranked circulation allows it to charge advertisers a premium, said feedback from advertisers shows they regard the Daily Telegraph's subscription sales as more valuable than sales generated by promotions because subscriptions involve a longterm commitment from readers.
Also at question, is how many buyers of newspapers offering special promotions are actually reading the paper -- and seeing the ads.

The Telegraph said it estimated that circulation for the Times dropped off by 185,000 after the Eurostar promotion stopped, falling from a high of 948,000 at the peak of the Eurostar promotion to 861,931.
